question: A 32-year-old woman with primary infertility for 2 years has normal ovarian reserve on TVS. The clinician now wants to assess tubal patency. Which investigation is the most appropriate first-line choice?

answers.text: MRI pelvis — it gives the best soft-tissue contrast for tubal pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI cannot reliably assess tubal patency. It does not visualise contrast flow through the tubes and is not a first-line investigation for tubal factor infertility.

answers.text: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) performed in the follicular phase — it outlines the uterine cavity and confirms tubal patency with contrast spill

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HSG in the follicular phase (days 7–10) is the standard first-line test for tubal patency. It images both the uterine cavity and tubal lumen, and free peritoneal spillage of contrast confirms patent tubes.

answers.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation as the initial investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Laparoscopy with dye test is the gold standard but is invasive. It is reserved for cases where HSG is inconclusive, shows apparent blockage, or where additional pelvic pathology (endometriosis, adhesions) is suspected.

answers.text: Transvaginal ultrasound with saline infusion — it is radiation-free and equally accurate as HSG for tubal patency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Saline infusion sonography (SIS) assesses the uterine cavity well but is not reliable for tubal patency. HSG remains the standard for tubal assessment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the modality-to-factor matching: tubal patency = HSG (follicular phase, contrast spill = patent); ovarian reserve = TVS (antral follicle count) or AMH; cavity = SIS or hysteroscopy.
Correct. HSG in the follicular phase is the first-line test for tubal factor: it assesses both the uterine cavity (polyps, septa, adhesions) and tubal patency in one radiation-minimal investigation.
